title: X‑Ray Discovery Uncovers 100‑Million‑Year‑Old Dinosaur‑Era Flower Fossil】
body:
A fossilized flower, preserved in exquisite detail for more than 100 million years, has been unveiled through high‑resolution X‑ray imaging, offering an unprecedented glimpse into the reproductive structures of early angiosperms during the age of the dinosaurs. The specimen, recovered from mid‑Cretaceous sedimentary rock in western Canada, is the oldest known flower to retain both pollen‑bearing organs and a fully formed ovary, challenging long‑standing assumptions about how quickly flowering plants diversified after their emergence.

The research team, comprising paleobotanists from the United States and the United Kingdom, employed synchrotron‑based X‑ray tomography to peer through the rock matrix without damaging the delicate fossil. The resulting three‑dimensional reconstruction revealed a petite, radially symmetric blossom roughly 5 mm in diameter, complete with five sepals, five petals, a central cluster of stamens, and a pistil containing an ovary with two ovules. Such a complete suite of floral parts had never been observed in a fossil of this age; previous Cretaceous specimens were typically fragmentary, preserving only isolated pollen grains or leaf impressions.

The discovery carries weighty implications for the evolutionary timeline of angiosperms. Molecular clock studies have long suggested that the origin of flowering plants predates their first appearance in the fossil record by tens of millions of years, but direct evidence has been scarce. This flower, dating to approximately 100 million years ago, pushes back the documented presence of fully formed reproductive structures to the middle of the Cretaceous, a period traditionally dominated by conifers, cycads, and the early rise of dinosaurs. Its morphology aligns closely with that of modern basal eudicots, indicating that key innovations—such as a differentiated perianth and a bicarpellate ovary—were already in place much earlier than previously thought.

The find also sheds light on the ecological dynamics of the time. The plant likely inhabited a warm, humid floodplain, coexisting with a diverse assemblage of herbivorous dinosaurs and early pollinating insects. The presence of a well‑developed flower suggests that insect pollination, rather than wind, may have already been a significant driver of plant reproduction in the Cretaceous, supporting hypotheses that the rapid radiation of angiosperms was closely linked to the diversification of pollinating insects. Moreover, the fossil’s preservation within fine‑grained mudstone points to rapid burial in a low‑oxygen environment, conditions that favor the retention of delicate organic structures over geological timescales.

While the study resolves a crucial gap in the fossil record, it also raises fresh questions. How widespread were such fully formed flowers across the Cretaceous world? Did they dominate certain habitats while remaining rare in others? And what genetic pathways underpinned the swift evolution of complex floral architectures? Future investigations using similar non‑destructive imaging techniques on other Cretaceous deposits could uncover a broader spectrum of early angiosperm diversity, helping to map the tempo and mode of flower evolution.

As the scientific community continues to refine its understanding of plant history, this 100‑million‑year‑old blossom stands as a vivid reminder that the deep past still holds secrets waiting to be revealed. By combining cutting‑edge technology with classic fieldwork, researchers are not only rewriting the story of how flowers first bloomed but also setting the stage for new insights into the intertwined evolution of plants, insects, and the megafauna that once roamed the Earth.
